body.head: Theatrical Examiner
body.p: On Wednesday week was revived Shakspeare's elegant play of Measure for Measure, for the purpose of introducing Mrs. Siddons once more to the public in her old part of Isabel, before that final farewell to the stage, which she means to take with the close of the present season. A high tone of morality has been assumed by the present able theatrical critic of the Times; and Measure for Measure has been stigmatized by him as "the most offensive play in the English language, there being nothing in the vulgarity of Jonson, or the outrageous coarseness of Massinger, or the intemperate humour of Beaumont and Fletcher, which can compare with the offence of Measure for Measure." We are afraid that the critic is new in the study of our ancient drama. Massinger, it is true, is often coarse, and almost every one of his plays is more offensive than Measure for Measure: the humour of Beaumont and Fletcher, it is true, is often intemperate; but Measure for Measure is "poison in jest," compared with much of the "offence" of Beaumont and Fletcher's "plays." But it is not true that Jonson is vulgar: on the contrary, his plays were greatly too refined for his audience: Jonson was on that account, like his great namesake of our times, "never a favourite with the public;" and some of his learned plays were actually damned; for instance, the Alchemist, the most exquisite comedy in the English language. We would not damp the honest warmth of indignant morality; but let not the critic deceive himself:—Measure for Measure is not, "beyond any competition, the most offensive play in the English language." Did the critic ever wade through the muck and filth of Dekkar, Ford, and the rest?—But we are glad to get at some standard of indecency, which the next sentence of the critique betrays to our view. "The plot is founded on an incident, which it would require the most dexterous contrivance of the most delicate language to convey." So then this is all: every body knows the plot of Measure for Measure, and every body discusses it freely: we would otherwise tell our readers, for fear they should think it was something worse, that this is the plot of the play:—A lover anticipates the privileges of a husband with his mistress, or in the plain but not indecent language of the play, "gets her with child" before marriage; and an obsolete statute of Vienna is raked out by the Duke's vicegerent, which declares the offence death. The sister of the criminal visits the Judge as an intercessor for her brother; and the Judge, smitten with her beauty, commits (or fancies he commits) the same crime towards the sister, for which he had sentenced the brother to die. It is needless to enter further into the nodus of the play; this is the groundwork of the plot, and this is the head and front of its offending, in point of indecency. Claudio was always intended, and was always prepared, to marry Juliet; and what does the poet represent the parties to gain by their imprudent anticipation of that marriage?—pleasure and comfort?—No; trouble, anxiety, and almost death. Is the man a libertine, or the woman abandoned? They are sufficiently punished for their crimes if they are. But the contrary is the case: his desire to marry her is not abated; and her principles are not relaxed because she is not married to him. Seduction is not glossed by this play, nor intrigue sanctioned. Instead of "the most offensive play in" sure. The Duke even commands that the boasted victim of Lucio's gallantry shall be discovered, and be compelled to marry her. We are not prepared to defend the conversations which pass between Mrs. Overdone, Elbow, the Clown, and Lucio: much of their language would be baneful in a theatre, if it were not obsolete; but their parts are not essential to the piece, the main story of which, "that cannot (forsooth) be expressed in society," has been a favourite with all ages and nations, has been commented upon by Mrs. Griffith, by Dr. Johnson, and by many other delicate and rigid critics, without ever being suspected of indecency, till the critic of a daily newspaper made the alarming discovery, which he announced to the public on the 30th day of October, 1811. For our parts, we do not think it augurs well for a nation to affect such a fastidious over-niceness. Some people's ears, as Mrs. Honour says, are the most delicate parts about them. The flagrancy of immorality is not diminished by cloaking its description in pretty "holiday and lady terms;" and many a fine Miss, who has turned away from the reading of her marriage settlements, because they talked of the children of her said husband on the body of his said wife lawfully to be begotten, has not scrupled to be afterwards faithless to her husband's bed. The morality of this country has not been found to increase since the French word amour has been prayed in aid to gloss over the licentiousness of Englishmen. We confess that we listen with honest pride to the plain unvarnishing and unextenuating language of our old comedies: we have no objection to hear these things called by their right names; and fancy ourselves for a moment carried back to the open simplicity of our forefathers. Softening the name of a vice is the surest road to soften the guilt and horror of it. So far from "disgusting and repelling "a British public," we are of opinion that Measure for Measure will prove one of the most interesting of Shakspeare revivals: the plot teems with event, and the blank verse is perhaps more full of passages to quote than any other of Shakspeare's plays. Dr. Johnson says of Measure for Measure that "the light or comic part is very natural and pleasing, but the grave scenes, if a few passages be excepted, have more labour than elegance." Now, of the light or comic part, Lucio appears to us a poor copy of Mercutio, and Elbow of Dogberry. It is the grave argument and eloquence which will always carry this play through the stage, the suspension of the interest, and the poetical justice and satisfactory result of the whole fable.

What critic cannot say that Mrs. Siddons looked thirty years too old for the part of Isabel? It was not to be expected—but she must have done so. But her performance! In her golden days of youth and beauty, Isabel must have been her chef d'œuvre, just as now her Lady Macbeth is. Her appeal to the returning Duke was irresistible; but when she dropped on her knees, and asked for justice, justice, justice, we thought that she should have dwelt on the retriplication of that word with one breath, and in one tone, as the only thing in her heart and on her lips, and not have paused and changed her voice and attitude between each recurrence of the word.

Mr. Kemble was dignified and sensible in the Duke; but we wanted him in Angelo too: that character was beyond Mr. Barrymore; he can play a mere tyrant with very passable bluster; but he could not paint the progress of Angelo's passion for Isabel. He gave some of his ar the English language,—in point of story and real event, we do not know a more moral play than Measure for Measure; with good discretion nevertheless; but why did not Mr. Young perform the character? Mr. Kemble chose the part of the Duke, we suppose, for its greater variety of dress and splendour of effect. His Monk was a finished portrait; and he worked the machinery of his ducal robes with much skill, if he would but hide this petty art. Mr. Jones wagged his hips in Lucio to little effect; but Mr. Liston's Clown was excellent. We were glad to see, too, that the character of Bernardine was not obliterated, but placed in the able hands of Mr. Emery. These are the things that bring Shakspeare's plays home to the life: every prison has its Bernardine; but no dramatist, except Shakspeare, would have ventured to touch so apparently disgusting an object. The fine ladies cry out against his intrusion; but show us human nature as it is, in all its degeneracies, in all its depravities, provided Shakspeare be the dramatist.
